'''Juan Max Dixon''' (born October 9, 1978) is an American former professional [[basketball]] player and former head coach for [[Coppin State University]] in [[Baltimore]].  Dixon led the [[Maryland Terrapins men's basketball|Maryland Terrapins]] to their first [[National Collegiate Athletic Association|NCAA]] championship in 2002 and earned [[NCAA basketball tournament Most Outstanding Player|Most Outstanding Player]] honors at the [[2002 Final Four]].

==Early life==
Dixon was born in [[Baltimore, Maryland]], where he attended [[Lake Clifton High School]] as a freshman.<ref name="The Baltimore Sun">{{cite news|url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/1997/01/05/a-star-already-tempered-by-life-boys-basketball-calvert-halls-juan-dixon-headed-for-maryland-next-season-is-admired-not-only-for-his-on-court-skills-but-for-the-way-he-and-his-family-have-dealt-with-s/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101020084712/http://articles.baltimoresun.com/1997-01-05/sports/1997005162_1_dixon-shooter-calvert-hall|url-status=live|archive-date=October 20, 2010|title=Calvert Hall's Juan Dixon, headed for Maryland next season, is admired not only for his on-court skills, but for the way he -- and his family -- have dealt with some tough challenges| work=The Baltimore Sun| last=Satterfield|first=Lem|date=January 5, 1997}}</ref> He then attended and played basketball at [[Calvert Hall College High School|Calvert Hall]], a high school in [[Towson, Maryland]]. While at Calvert Hall, he scored 1,590 career points under the tutelage of head coach Mark Amatucci.

Both his mother, Juanita, and father, Phil, were addicted to [[heroin]], and died of [[AIDS]]-related illnesses before Dixon was 17 years old.<ref name="Chicago Tribune">{{cite news|url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/2002/03/28/marylands-juan-dixon-has-overcome-a-perilous-childhood-and-his-parents-deaths-to-become-one-of-the-nations-top-players/|title=Maryland's Juan Dixon has overcome a perilous childhood and his parents' deaths to become one of the nation's top players | work=Chicago Tribune | first=Skip|last=Myslenski|date=March 28, 2002}}</ref>  He was then raised by his grandparents Roberta and Warnick Graves in Baltimore.

Dixon's aunt, [[Sheila Dixon]], was the mayor of Baltimore.<ref>{{cite web|last=Washington |first=The |url=http://washingtontimes.com/metro/20070117-101644-9729r.htm |title=Dixon elevated to Baltimore mayor |work=Washington Times |date=2007-01-17 |access-date=2011-11-05}}</ref>  Dixon's [[half brother]] is Jermaine Dixon, who played shooting guard for the [[University of Pittsburgh]] [[Pittsburgh Panthers|Panthers]] basketball team.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://pittsburghpanthers.cstv.com/sports/m-baskbl/mtt/dixon_jermaine00.html |title=Player Bio: Jermaine Dixon – PittsburghPanthers.com – University of Pittsburgh Official Athletic Site |publisher=Pittsburghpanthers.cstv.com |date=1987-04-15 |access-date=2011-11-05}}</ref> His second cousin Brandon Driver played cornerback for the [[San Jose State University|San Jose State]] [[San Jose State Spartans football|Spartans]] football team.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.sjsuspartans.com/ViewArticle.dbml?SPSID=29302&SPID=2290&DB_LANG=C&DB_OEM_ID=5600&ATCLID=204765424&Q_SEASON=2011 |title=Brandon Driver – SJSUSpartans.com – Official Web Site of San Jose State Athletics |publisher=SJSU Spartans |date=1987-09-09 |access-date=2011-11-05 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120325111536/http://www.sjsuspartans.com/ViewArticle.dbml?SPSID=29302&SPID=2290&DB_LANG=C&DB_OEM_ID=5600&ATCLID=204765424&Q_SEASON=2011 |archive-date=2012-03-25 }}</ref>  In 2016, Juan Dixon discovered that Phil Dixon was not his biological father, and that his biological father Bruce Flanigan was still alive.  Flanigan had an affair with Juanita Dixon while she was separated from Phil, and a blood test confirmed his paternity.  Dixon and Flanigan reconnected and became good friends.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2016/11/26/juan-dixon-forges-relationship-with-the-father-he-didnt-know-existed/ |title=Juan Dixon forges relationship with the father he didn't know existed |last=Markus |first=Don |date=November 26, 2016  |work=The Baltimore Sun |access-date=April 6, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://play.hbogo.com/feature/urn:hbo:feature:GWIjITwqLHqmywwEAAAIn|title=HBO GO®. It's HBO. Anywhere.®|website=HBO GO®|access-date=25 September 2018}}</ref>

===Personal life===
Dating since 1996, Dixon married his high-school sweetheart, Robyn Bragg, in July 2005.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2005/07/30/ex-terp-dixon-weds-today-may-also-say-i-do-to-portland/|title=Ex-Terp Dixon weds today, may also say 'I do' to Portland|date=30 July 2005 |access-date=25 September 2018}}</ref> She works in the public relations field and was a cast member in the Bravo reality television show ''[[The Real Housewives of Potomac]]'' from 2016 to 2024. They have two sons, Corey (b. 2008) and Carter (b. 2010). The two divorced in March 2012 but still lived together in [[Maryland]] after their divorce.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2012/03/31/10-years-after-the-national-title-juan-dixon-says-hes-going-to-get-back-to-the-nba/|title=10 years after the national title, Juan Dixon says he's 'going to get back to the NBA'|date=31 March 2012 |access-date=25 September 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://washingtonian.com/2014/01/30/the-beauty-diaries/|title=The Beauty Diaries - Washingtonian|date=30 January 2014|access-date=25 September 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.bravotv.com/the-daily-dish/real-housewives-of-potomac-robyn-dixon&ved=0ahUKEwi36tDF7L_KAhWJHx4KHd8SCuAQFggbMAA&usg=AFQjCNEjvkf1XrYbw7Y-8Jce7clXay-p_A&sig2=xjO2Ga6AQ5WwOn8A9chVZQ |title= Real Housewives of Potomac: Who is Robyn Dixon? | the Daily Dish|website=www.bravotv.com |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160119032054/http://www.bravotv.com/the-daily-dish/real-housewives-of-potomac-robyn-dixon |archive-date=2016-01-19}}</ref> In August 2022, the couple remarried.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Robyn Dixon and Juan Dixon Are Married Again! RHOP to Air Surprise Wedding in Season 7 Finale |url=https://people.com/tv/real-housewives-of-potomac-robyn-dixon-juan-dixon-married-again/ |access-date=2023-01-23 |website=Peoplemag |language=en}}</ref>

==Playing career==

===College===
Dixon arrived at the [[University of Maryland, College Park]] after head coach [[Gary Williams]] inadvertently discovered him at an [[Amateur Athletic Union|AAU]] tournament in Georgia. Williams watched as Dixon dove for the ball down 20 points with two minutes to go. Williams was impressed by the effort.<ref>"Sweet Redemption", by Gary Williams, David A Vise (2002)</ref>

Dixon played in 34 games his freshman year and averaged 7.4 points per game. He made improvements in his sophomore year as he averaged 18 points per game and was selected to the [[1999–2000 Maryland Terrapins men's basketball team#Accolades 2|1999–2000 All-ACC team]].

Both Dixon and the Terps entered the 2000–01 season with high expectations. The Terps began ranked in the top ten in most major polls while Dixon was a candidate for the Naismith Award Player of the Year award and the Wooden Award Player of the Year award. Dixon helped lead the Terps to their first ever [[Final Four]] appearance where the team lost to [[Duke Blue Devils men's basketball|Duke]]. Dixon ended the season averaging 18.2 points per game and was again elected to the All-ACC first team.

Maryland began the 2001–02 season ranked #2 in [[ESPN/USA Today Coaches' poll|ESPN/USA Today Coaches' Poll]]. Dixon led the Terps to a 32–4 record and the school's first ever [[2002 NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament|National Championship]]. He was voted to All-ACC team and was also a first team All-American. He was also recognized as one of the nation's best college players and was honored as the 2002 [[ACC Men's Basketball Player of the Year]] and [[ACC Athlete of the Year]].

He became Maryland men's basketball's all-time leading scorer when he scored 29 points against Wisconsin to help Maryland advance to the Sweet Sixteen, passing [[Len Bias]] (2,149 points).  He also became the only player in [[National Collegiate Athletic Association|NCAA]] history to accumulate 2,000 points, 300 steals and 200 [[three-point field goal]]s. In addition to leaving Maryland as the highest-scoring men's player, Dixon also left as the school's all-time men's leader in three-pointers made (239) and attempted (615).  He is second on Maryland's all-time steals list with 333 and third in free-throw percentage (.850).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://umterps.com/documents/2020/4/20/MBK_Record_Book.pdf|title=MBK Record Book (PDF)|website=University of Maryland Athletics|language=en|access-date=2020-04-28}}</ref>  Dixon also stands as Maryland's all-time NCAA Tournament scoring leader with 294.  Upon completion of his career, Dixon's #3 jersey was honored and now hangs in the [[Xfinity Center (College Park, Maryland)|Xfinity Center]].  In 2002, Juan Dixon was honored as a part of the [[ACC 50th Anniversary men's basketball team]], one of only 8 Terrapins selected to the 50-man team. After his senior season, Dixon was featured on the cover of a video game, ''[[NCAA Final Four 2003]]''.

===NBA===
[[Image:J Dixon - Wizards vs Heat 2009-04-04.jpg|thumb|right|180px|Dixon as a member of the Washington Wizards.]]
Dixon was drafted 17th overall by the [[Washington Wizards]] in the [[2002 NBA draft]]. He spent the first three years of his NBA career with the Wizards. In his third season in Washington ([[2004–05 NBA season|2004–05]]), he averaged eight points per game, including a career-high 35 points in Game 4 of the Eastern Conference Quarterfinals against the [[Chicago Bulls]]. Dixon signed as a [[free agent]] with the [[Portland Trail Blazers]] during the summer of 2005. Soon after, his Wizards and Terrapins teammate and friend [[Steve Blake]] signed with Portland as well. In his first game back in [[Washington, D.C.|D.C.]], Dixon was given a standing ovation from the [[Capital One Arena|Verizon Center]] crowd upon coming off the bench towards the end of the first quarter.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.sportsline.com/nba/gamecenter/recap/NBA_20051130_POR@WAS |title=Wizards 96, Blazers 89 |work=Sportsline |date=2008-06-11 |access-date=2011-11-05 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071205172600/http://www.sportsline.com/nba/gamecenter/recap/NBA_20051130_POR%40WAS |archive-date=2007-12-05 }}</ref> In Dixon's first year with the Blazers, he started 42 times and played in 76 games. In his last year with the Wizards, he only started four games and played in 63. He also increased his, assists, and shooting percentage considerably in Portland. However, he was later traded at the 2007 NBA trade deadline to Toronto for [[Fred Jones (basketball)|Fred Jones]] and future considerations.<ref>{{cite web|author=The Official Site of the Portland Trail Blazers |url=http://www.nba.com/blazers/news/fred-211975-1218.html |title=Portland acquires Fred Jones from Toronto, send Dixon to Raptors |publisher=NBA |access-date=2011-11-05}}</ref>

On the 2008 NBA [[trade deadline]], February 21, 2008, Dixon was traded from the [[Toronto Raptors]] to the [[Detroit Pistons]] in exchange for [[Center (basketball)|center]] [[Primož Brezec]] and cash considerations.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://network.nationalpost.com/np/blogs/postedsports/archive/2008/02/21/nba-raptors-deal-juan-dixon.aspx |title=NBA: Raptors deal Dixon |access-date=2008-02-21 }}{{dead link|date=October 2025|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref>

On September 24, 2008, the Washington Wizards signed Dixon to a partially guaranteed one-year deal for $1.03 million, the veterans' minimum for a player with Dixon's experience.

Dixon's final NBA game was on April 15, 2009, in a 107–115 loss to the [[Boston Celtics]] where he recorded 3 points, 1 rebound, 2 assists and 2 steals. On September 28, 2009, Juan Dixon signed a contract with the [[Atlanta Hawks]]. He was waived October 20, 2009.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2008/09/23/AR2008092303578.html |title=Wizards Bring Back Dixon |newspaper=Washington Post |date= 2008-09-24|access-date=2011-11-05 |first=Ivan |last=Carter}}</ref>

===Europe===
On November 1, 2009, Dixon signed with [[Aris B.C.|Aris Thessaloniki]] of the [[A1 Ethniki|Greek A1 League]].<ref name="arisbc.gr">[http://www.arisbc.gr/index.php?SCREEN=page&PageID=2304&LangID=1 Στον Άρη ο Χουάν Ντίξον] {{in lang|el}}</ref> The next season, he joined [[Unicaja Málaga]] of Spain. In February 2010, he was suspended indefinitely by [[FIBA]] after testing positive for steroids.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.usatoday.com/sports/basketball/2010-02-13-2145867695_x.htm |title=Former NBA player banned after steroid test |work=Usa Today |date=2010-02-13 |access-date=2011-11-05}}</ref> In March 2011, he signed with [[Bandırma Banvit]] in Turkey.<ref>[http://www.tbl.org.tr/beko/haber_detay.asp?Haber=9201&sezon=2010-2011 Banvit, Juan Dixon İle Anlaştı] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110313012232/http://www.tbl.org.tr/beko/haber_detay.asp?Haber=9201 |date=2011-03-13 }} {{in lang|tr}}</ref> He played one season before entering the coaching profession.

==Coaching career==
[[File:Juan Dixon at Coppin State.jpg|thumb|Dixon coaching Coppin State]]
On November 27, 2013, Dixon joined the [[Maryland Terrapins men's basketball|Maryland Terrapin]] coaching staff as a special assistant under head coach [[Mark Turgeon]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Markus |first=Don |url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2013/11/27/juan-dixon-to-join-terps-mens-basketball-staff-as-special-assistant/ |title=Dixon to join Terps men's basketball staff as special assistant |work=Baltimore Sun |date=2013-11-27 |access-date=2013-11-27 |archive-date=June 29, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140629133553/http://www.baltimoresun.com/sports/terps/tracking-the-terps/bal-terps-basketball-juan-dixon-dalonte-hill-dustin-clark-20131127,0,7640382.story |url-status=live }}</ref> In July 2016, Dixon was relieved of his duties.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/story/_/id/16825559|title=Terps relieve ex-star Dixon of assistant duties|date=6 July 2016|website=ESPN.com|access-date=25 September 2018}}</ref>

On October 14, 2016, Dixon was hired as head coach of the women's basketball team at the University of the District of Columbia (UDC).<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/dc-sports-bog/wp/2016/10/14/former-terps-star-juan-dixon-hired-as-udc-womens-basketball-coach/|title=Former Terps star Juan Dixon hired as UDC women's basketball coach|newspaper=Washington Post|access-date=2017-02-17}}</ref> After a 3–25 season, he was hired as men's head coach at [[Coppin State Eagles men's basketball|Coppin State]].<ref>{{cite news|first=Don|last=Markus|title=Former Terp Juan Dixon to be next men's basketball coach at Coppin State|url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2017/04/22/former-terp-juan-dixon-to-be-next-mens-basketball-coach-at-coppin-state/|newspaper=[[Baltimore Sun]]|date=April 22, 2017|access-date=April 22, 2017}}</ref> After 6 seasons earning only 51 wins as a division one head coach, he was fired in March 2023.<ref>{{Cite web | title=Coppin State Fires Menâs Basketball Coach Juan Dixon, per Report | url=https://www.si.com/college/2023/03/15/coppin-state-fires-mens-basketball-coach-juan-dixon | access-date=2026-09-06 | website=www.si.com | date=March 15, 2023 }}</ref>

In the summer of 2025, Dixon was named the head coach of Maryland's alumni basketball team, Shell Shock, in [[The Basketball Tournament]]. Behind Dixon's leadership, Shell Shock won the James Madison Regional and advanced to the Elite Eight, before losing to Best Virginia, West Virginia's alumni team.
